title: Class 11 Chemistry — Aromatic Hydrocarbons Study Guide
notes: Aromatic compounds are cyclic, planar, conjugated systems with delocalized π electrons and unusual stability. Hückel's rule predicts aromaticity for a planar, fully conjugated monocycle with (4n+2) π electrons. Benzene has six π electrons (n=1). Kekulé drawings show alternating bonds, but all C–C bonds are equivalent because π electrons are delocalized; the ring is not a set of localized alternating bonds.

Syllabus preparations of benzene include decarboxylation of sodium benzoate with soda lime, deoxygenation of phenol using zinc dust, and trimerization of ethyne under suitable conditions. Benzene is volatile, flammable and toxic; avoid inhalation and skin exposure. Its high carbon content gives a luminous smoky flame on combustion.

Benzene usually undergoes electrophilic aromatic substitution because substitution restores aromaticity. The steps are electrophile generation, attack to form a resonance-stabilized sigma complex, then loss of H⁺ to restore the ring. Nitration uses a nitronium electrophile generated from concentrated acids; halogenation and Friedel–Crafts reactions use Lewis-acid catalysts. Sulphonation is reversible under suitable conditions. Addition such as hydrogenation can occur under forcing conditions but sacrifices aromatic stabilization.

A substituent affects both rate and position of a second substitution. Electron-donating groups generally activate and direct ortho/para; many electron-withdrawing groups deactivate and direct meta. Halogens are an important exception: they deactivate inductively but direct ortho/para by resonance donation. Steric effects and multiple substituents may complicate predictions.

Disubstituted benzene has ortho (1,2-), meta (1,3-) and para (1,4-) arrangements. Draw and number the ring clearly. In reaction answers identify the electrophile, catalyst and restoration of aromaticity; distinguish substitution from addition across a localized alkene-like bond.
formulas: Hückel criterion: (4n + 2) delocalized π electrons, n = 0,1,2,…
C₆H₆ + HNO₃ → C₆H₅NO₂ + H₂O (conc. H₂SO₄ catalyst/medium)
keyPoints: Benzene has six delocalized π electrons and equivalent C–C bonds.
Electrophilic substitution preserves aromaticity after H⁺ is lost.
Electron donors generally direct ortho/para; many withdrawing groups direct meta; halogens deactivate but direct ortho/para.
Ortho, meta and para denote 1,2-, 1,3- and 1,4-disubstitution.
Benzene is toxic and flammable; laboratory handling requires proper controls.
practiceQuestions: Apply Hückel's rule to benzene and explain equivalent C–C bond lengths.
Describe nitration stages and identify its electrophile.
Predict directing effects of –CH₃, –NO₂ and –Cl in a second substitution.
Draw and name the ortho, meta and para isomers of dichlorobenzene.
List three syllabus preparations of benzene and state one hazard.
summary: Benzene's aromatic stabilization favors substitution over ordinary addition. Apply Hückel's rule and use electrophile, catalyst and substituent directing effects to predict products.
